messages.subject: Prediction changes the estimates! why?
parts:
So I was working with some time series and I found that if I fitted 20 years of data I was getting certain estimates but if I was fitting 19 years of data and wanted to predict the last year of data, then the estimates for all the years differed a little. I did not think much of it, but when i included the space component to my model then I got things drastically different.

So I thought it was my code. 

To figure out what went wrong I started a the beginning and decided to look at the example in the R-INAL webpage

Here is the code I ran:

## Load the data
require(INLA)
data(Tokyo)
summary(Tokyo)

Tokyo$y1 <- Tokyo$y
Tokyo$y1[300:366] <- NA

## Define the model
# all the data
formula = y ~ f(time, model="rw2", cyclic=TRUE, param=c(1,0.0001)) - 1
# partial data without the prediction part
formulapart = y[1:299] ~ f(time, model="rw2", cyclic=TRUE, param=c(1,0.0001)) - 1
# the partial data with the prediction part
formulapred = y1 ~ f(time, model="rw2", cyclic=TRUE, param=c(1,0.0001)) - 1


## The call to inca

result = inla(formula, family="binomial", Ntrials=n, data=Tokyo, 
              control.predictor=list(compute=T))
resultpart = inla(formulapart, family="binomial", Ntrials=n, data=Tokyo[1:299,], 
              control.predictor=list(compute=T))

# two methods of predictions
link = rep(NA, nrow(Tokyo))
link[which(is.na(Tokyo$y1))] = 1
resultpred = inla(formulapred, family="binomial", Ntrials=n, data=Tokyo, 
              control.predictor=list(compute=T)) 
resultpredL = inla(formulapred, family="binomial", Ntrials=n, data=Tokyo, 
                  control.predictor=list(compute=T, link = link)) 

summary(result)
summary(result part)
# this two below give the same (good)
summary(resultpred)
summary(resultpredL)


# The estimates for the RW2 for the 20 first data points (not the predicted)
cbind(result$summary.random$time[1:20,2],
      resultpart$summary.random$time[1:20,2],
      resultpred$summary.random$time[1:20,2],
      resultpredL$summary.random$time[1:20,2])

           [,1]      [,2]      [,3]      [,4]
 [1,] -1.808871 -1.087086 -1.514536 -1.514533

[11,] -1.770045 -1.434036 -1.660000 -1.659999
[12,] -1.769744 -1.465083 -1.673585 -1.673585
[13,] -1.769720 -1.494863 -1.686601 -1.686601
[14,] -1.769957 -1.523384 -1.699039 -1.699039
[15,] -1.770477 -1.550704 -1.710929 -1.710930
[16,] -1.771334 -1.576942 -1.722344 -1.722344
[17,] -1.772505 -1.602111 -1.733277 -1.733278
[18,] -1.773999 -1.626277 -1.743762 -1.743763
[19,] -1.775858 -1.649559 -1.753872 -1.753873
[20,] -1.778049 -1.671969 -1.763600 -1.763601

As one can see while the two prediction methods do agree on the estimates for the RW2, but they differ from the ones obtained when we fitted the model without the NA! I thought the estimates would be based on the portion of data that was given so maybe they would be the same as if the NA did not exist but no, they are different form those two...

what is going here? why asking to predict in the future (e.g. one more year of data) would change the estimates for the past (the 20 years of data that help build the model in the first place)?

Thank you
Sab.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Prediction changes the estimates! why?
parts:
Have you checked the constraint settings for the rw2 model? When a sum-to-zero constrain is applied, it’s applied to the whole model component, so the size of the model matters; for example, a model with 20 timepoints and missing values for the last 10 is not the same model as a model that only has the first 10 timepoints.
This is an inherent issue that is particularly common when intrinsic models are used (but you’ll need to check if this is what’s happening in this particular case). To avoid that issue, look at the total prediction instead of the model component.

Finn

I dont think it is the constraint.

Here is another example i played with this morning. It is based on Ruiz-Cárdenas, Krainski, and Rue (2012) about the dynamic models. I took their example 1 of  simple dynamic model and made sure to specify “const = F” and it is still doing the same thing

here is the comparative output for the  betas

and i also attached the R file if you want to run it on your side. But her tis the code

####################################################################
####     EXAMPLE 1  from Ruiz-Cárdenas,Krainski, and Rue (2012) ####
####################################################################


## Simulating a Poisson dynamic regression (p1814)
## (dynamic intercept and two dynamic regrressors)
## -----------------------------------------------
require(INLA)
set.seed(123456)


n <- 300
x1 <- runif(n)
x2 <- runif(n)
W0 = 0.005
W1 = 0.01
W2 <- 0.005
w0 <- rnorm(n,0,sqrt(W0))
w1 <- rnorm(n,0,sqrt(W1))
w2 <- rnorm(n,0,sqrt(W2))
y <- b0 <- b1 <- b2 <- numeric(n)
b0[1] <- 3 + w0[1]
b1[1] <- 0 + w1[1]
b2[1] <- 0 + w2[1]
for (t in 2:n){
  b0[t] <- b0[t-1] + w0[t]
  b1[t] <- b1[t-1] + w1[t]
  b2[t] <- b2[t-1] + w2[t]
}
y <- rpois(n,exp(b0 + b1*x1 + b2*x2))
y1 <- y
y1[276:300] <- NA




data <- data.frame(x1, x2, y, y1)


# defining indices for rw1 coefficients
# -------------------------------------
id <- 1:n    # indices for beta_0
id1 <- 1:n   # indices for beta_1
id2 <- 1:n   # indices for beta_2




# formulating the model
# ---------------------
# formulation with default hyperprior for all the data
formula <- y ~ f(id, model="rw1",constr=F) +
  f(id1, x1, model="rw1",constr=F) +
  f(id2, x2, model="rw1",constr=F) -1
# formulation with default hyperprior for all the data[1:275] and NA[276:300]
link = rep(NA, nrow(data))
link[which(is.na(data$y1))] = 1
formulaPRED <- y1 ~ f(id, model="rw1",constr=F) +
  f(id1, x1, model="rw1",constr=F) +
  f(id2, x2, model="rw1",constr=F) -1


# call to fit the model
# ---------------------
# Fitting all 300 data points
r <- inla(formula, family="poisson", data = data.frame(id,id1,id2,data),
          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))


# Fitting the first 274 and have the last 25
rPRED <- inla(formulaPRED, family="poisson", data = data.frame(id,id1,id2,data),
          control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link = link))


# Compare the output of the non-predicted part
intercepts <- cbind(r$summary.random$id[1:20,2],
      rPRED$summary.random$id[1:20,2])
betahat1s <- cbind(r$summary.random$id1[1:20,2],
      rPRED$summary.random$id1[1:20,2])
betahat2s <- cbind(r$summary.random$id2[1:20,2],
      rPRED$summary.random$id2[1:20,2])
comparison <- data.frame(intercepts, betahat1s, betahat2s)
colnames(comparison) <- c("B0hat","B0 w/ Pred",
                          "B1hat","B1 w/ Pred",
                          "B1hat","B1 w/ Pred")
comparison




I simulated n=300. fitted a simple RW1 dynamic model with all the data, and then with the data where I replaced the last 25 y by NA to have it predict. and when i compare the betas for the first 20 datapoint at the beginning of the model, they are not the same for any of them…. and those should not change since they are not part of the predicted portion

thank you for your help in trying to get the same betas estimates for the non-prediction portion, with and without prediction

SAB

numerical methods are not exact. would be cool if they were though.
Here is an example

for (n in c(10, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000)) {
A = matrix(rnorm(n^2), n, n); A = A %*% t(A)
B = matrix(10 + rnorm(n^2), n, n); B = B %*% t(B)
C = cbind(rbind(A + B, -B), rbind(-B, B))
print(c(n, format(mean(abs(solve(C)[1:n,1:n] - solve(A))), dig=8)))
}

where the first n-block of C^-1 *is* exactly A^-1, but numerically, the
abs difference is like

[1] "10" "2.8312418e-08"
[1] "50" "2.0001186e-09"
[1] "100" "6.5779975e-08"
[1] "250" "1.5011187e-05"
[1] "500" "2.0271233e-05"
[1] "1000" "4.9217048e-06"
>


this is what cause your issue in your case.


H

Thank you for your response.

here is how I came to think that something was not right with how INLA was predicting...

I am working on a model quite complex. R-INLA does a great job at fitting the model. However, I was given additional data and wanted to check how prediction was performing. and it is when i notice things started to be very off when i was considering space in addition than just time. When only time is in question the difference between the two cases (the original data and the data plus the NA of the new data to run the check) is minimal and I could live with it.


But exactly same model with the exception of three covariates and BYM space component and now things falls apart when I try to predict


Here is the great fit for one area when i am not doing prediction (the wiggling is due to the presence of the other covariate effects):


But with prediction in for just one sequence


Not only you can see that the prediction part is completely the wrong way, but it changed the model before that drastically.... So, i do understand that numerical approximations are not exact, and I was not troubled when I first tried to predict with just time but when the model is complex it seems to go beyond the mere approximation error. 


Or maybe the errors are cumulative, making prediction in the case of complex models not feasible?

But the part that was the most troubling me what that it changed the model itself so much when i try to predict that it rendered the fitting part not good anymore.


Hence, my reaching out to figure out on more simple example why I was seeing the exact same behavior or if it was something that i was missing when I was programming even a simple dynamic model.


Again thank you,


SAB.
